catalog_quote: All data are written phonemically. (') before a syllable indicates that stress falls on that syllable. ... 1.1 Stress Shift.¹ Primary stress always occurs on either the penultimate or ultimate syllable of a stem. Upon suffixation stress shifts according to the following rules. 1.1.1 Stress Remains on the Same Syllable. Stress does not shift upon suffixation on words with a CVC'CVC syllable pattern with ultimate stress except if this is a C₁eC₂'C₁eC₂ pattern. kog'kog + -en → kog'kogen 'to knock at something' qak'yat + -en → qak'yaten 'to climb over something' 1.1.2 Stress Shifts One Syllable. Upon the suffixation of -en or -an, stress shifts one syllable toward the suffix on the C₁eC₂'C₁eC₂ syllable pattern and all other syllable patterns except CVC'CVC. NOTE: the listed open_url (rosettaproject_ilk_phon-1) is the Rosetta chunk for entry 14, Ilongot (Kakiduge:n), p. 14 — wrong language; the correct chunk for xnn is rosettaproject_xnn_phon-1 (p. 24), which is what was read. The full 239-page book (word lists with stress marks) is not in the open excerpt.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The phonology summary lists 'Stress' as a phonological unit of Northern Kankanay (alongside the consonant and vowel inventories), i.e. the language has word stress that Reid/Hettick treat as a phonemic feature; nothing is said about where it falls, whether it is predictable, or about secondary stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Reid 1971 entry 24 describes the dialect of Balugan, Sagada, Mountain Province ('also referred to as Sagada Igorot, or Western Bontoc'), data from Donna Hettick 1966. Vanoverbergh 1917 (not opened) describes 'Lepanto Igorot as it is spoken at Bauco' (Bauko, Mountain Province), a different Northern Kankanay locality. The listed archive.org URL for Reid 1971 is actually the Ilongot (ilk) excerpt, not Northern Kankanay.

sources.quote: 'Kankanay data have been taken from various sources - Vanoverbergh 1933, Scott 1957, and Reid 1971. The latter two sources document the Northern Kankanay dialect as spoken respectively in Sagada town and in Balugan (Bugang) ... The dialects are not phonologically differentiated. All Kankanay forms are rewritten phonemically, with e representing a mid to high central vowel, and [accent mark] representing length on an open penultimate syllable.' I.e.
